title: Why no rank-k matrix does better
summary: The hard half of Eckart–Young: a small rank forces a null space that meets span(v₁…v_{k+1}).

blocks.title: The half that is left
blocks.body:
You proved the easy half: $A_k$, the SVD cut to $k$ terms, has $\|A - A_k\|_2 = \sigma_{k+1}$.

The hard half: **no** matrix $B$ of rank at most $k$ does better, so $\|A - B\|_2 \ge \sigma_{k+1}$.

Your idea is the proof: $B$'s null space is big, so it must meet span$(v_1, \ldots, v_{k+1})$. This lesson builds it, first in $\mathbb{R}^3$ with $k = 1$. The picture is the easy half, for a $2 \times 2$ matrix.

blocks.title: How big is B's null space?

define.meaning: For a matrix with $n$ columns, rank + dimension of the null space $= n$.

blocks.why: A small rank forces a big null space. That is the lever the proof pulls.
blocks.prompt: $B$ is $3 \times 3$ with rank 1. What is the dimension of its null space?
hints: Use rank + nullity = number of columns.

blocks.title: Two planes in ℝ³

define.meaning: All combinations of the first two right singular vectors of $A$: the directions $A$ stretches most.

blocks.why: If the two subspaces must share a non-zero vector, that vector is the witness the proof needs.
blocks.prompt: In $\mathbb{R}^3$, $B$'s null space (dimension 2) and span$(v_1, v_2)$ (dimension 2) meet in a subspace. What is the smallest dimension that meeting can have?
hints: Picture two planes through the origin in $\mathbb{R}^3$.
blocks.solution: At least 1: two planes through the origin always share a line. So there is a unit $w$ with $Bw = 0$ and $w$ in span$(v_1, v_2)$.
blocks.next: Do it for any n and k

blocks.title: Any n, any k
blocks.why: This is the step that makes it a proof for every matrix, not just this one.
blocks.prompt: In $\mathbb{R}^n$ with rank$(B) \le k$: $\dim N(B) \ge n - k$, and span$(v_1, \ldots, v_{k+1})$ has dimension $k + 1$. Add the two dimensions. Type the result in terms of $n$ (and $k$, if any is left).
blocks.solution: $n + 1 > n$, so the two subspaces of $\mathbb{R}^n$ share a non-zero vector. Scale it to a unit vector $w$: $Bw = 0$ and $w \in$ span$(v_1, \ldots, v_{k+1})$.

blocks.title: What w forces

define.meaning: $\|M\|_2$ is the largest $\|Mx\|$ over unit vectors $x$. So $\|M\|_2 \ge \|Mw\|$ for any one unit $w$.

blocks.why: Since $Bw = 0$, $(A - B)w = Aw$. So the error is at least $\|Aw\|$, and $\|Aw\|$ can't be small.
blocks.prompt: Take $A = \mathrm{diag}(3, 2, 1)$, so $\sigma = 3, 2, 1$ and $v_i = e_i$. A unit $w$ in span$(e_1, e_2)$ is $(a, b, 0)$ with $a^2 + b^2 = 1$. What is the smallest $\|Aw\|^2$ can be?
blocks.solution: 4, at $w = e_2$. In general $\|Aw\|^2 = \sum_i \sigma_i^2 (v_i \cdot w)^2 \ge \sigma_{k+1}^2$ for any unit $w$ in span$(v_1, \ldots, v_{k+1})$. So $\|A - B\|_2 \ge \|Aw\| \ge \sigma_{k+1}$.

blocks.title: A challenger
blocks.why: Running the argument on one real $B$ shows where the witness comes from.
blocks.prompt: Challenge it with the rank-1 $B = \begin{bmatrix}3&1&0\\0&0&0\\0&0&0\end{bmatrix}$. Find a non-zero $w$ with $Bw = 0$ and $w$ in span$(e_1, e_2)$, so its third entry is 0. Any multiple will do.

answer.acceptNote: Any non-zero multiple of $(1, -3, 0)$ is the same witness.

hints: With $w_1 = 1$, solve $3 + w_2 = 0$. The third entry is 0 because $w$ is in span$(e_1, e_2)$.

blocks.title: How the challenger does
blocks.why: The bound says this has to come out at least $\sigma_2^2 = 4$.
blocks.prompt: For $w = (1, -3, 0)$, compute $\|(A - B)w\|^2 / \|w\|^2$: the squared stretch along $w$.
blocks.solution: 4.5, at least 4 as promised. So $\|A - B\|_2 \ge \sqrt{4.5} > 2 = \|A - A_1\|_2$: this $B$ loses, as every rank-1 $B$ must.

blocks.title: The bound
blocks.why: Together with your easy half, this is the whole theorem.
blocks.prompt: So for every $B$ of rank at most 1, $\|A - B\|_2$ is at least what number, for $A = \mathrm{diag}(3, 2, 1)$?
hints: It is one of the singular values of $A$.
blocks.solution: $\sigma_2 = 2$, and $A_1$ reaches it. With your easy half, that is Eckart–Young in the 2-norm: the smallest $\|A - B\|_2$ over rank$(B) \le k$ is $\sigma_{k+1}$, reached by $A_k$.
